title: Use Scale Factors with Similar Shapes
description: Connect linear scale factors with perimeter, area, surface-area, and volume ratios, then move flexibly between those measurements for similar two- and three-dimensional shapes.

questions.stem_html: Two similar polygons have corresponding sides of length 4 and 7. The polygon with the side of length 4 has perimeter 40. What is the other perimeter?
questions.explanation_html: The multiplier from the first shape to the second is 7/4. Perimeter is a length, so multiply 40 by that factor once.
questions.variation: Scale perimeter linearly in the required direction

questions.stem_html: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides of lengths 3 and 5. The triangle with the side of length 3 has area 45. What is the other area?
questions.explanation_html: Square the linear multiplier 5/3. Applying that squared factor to area 45 gives \(125\).
questions.variation: Square the linear multiplier for area

questions.stem_html: Two similar figures have areas in the ratio 9 to 49. A side of the first figure has length 24. What is the corresponding side length of the second?
questions.explanation_html: Take square roots of the area ratio to recover the linear ratio 3 to 7. Apply the multiplier 7/3 to 24.
questions.variation: Recover a length multiplier from an area ratio

questions.stem_html: Two similar solids have corresponding edges of lengths 3 and 5. The solid with the edge of length 3 has volume 54. What is the volume of the other solid?
questions.explanation_html: Cube the linear multiplier 5/3, then multiply the original volume 54 by it.

questions.stem_html: Two similar solids have volumes in the ratio 27 to 125. The first has surface area 81. What is the surface area of the second?
questions.explanation_html: Take cube roots to recover the linear ratio 3 to 5. Then square the multiplier 5/3 and multiply the first surface area by it.
questions.variation: Convert a volume ratio to a surface-area result
